prospect.additionalContext: Utility: LoneStar Electric | Rate class: LGS-2 (Large General Service) | Blended rate: $0.1785/kWh | Monthly usage: 93,550 kWh | Peak demand: 487 kW | Billing period: Mar 14 – Apr 12, 2025

usageReduction.text: Implement a demand-focused HVAC controls sequence across the 15 floors: add optimum start/stop, weekend/after-hours setbacks, supply air temperature reset, and static pressure reset tied to occupancy. In Texas offices, these controls typically cut cooling energy and demand charges quickly, which is especially valuable at a 487 kW peak under an LGS-2 rate.
usageReduction.source: DOE Better Buildings: HVAC controls and scheduling savings; ASHRAE 90.1-2022 controls requirements

usageReduction.text: Audit the dedicated server room and isolate its cooling from the office HVAC system by tightening setpoints, adding hot/cold aisle containment if feasible, and using high-efficiency precision cooling or dedicated CRAC/VRF controls. Server rooms often run 24/7 and can drive a disproportionate share of base load and peak demand in office buildings.
usageReduction.source: DOE Better Buildings: Data center/server room efficiency guidance; U.S. DOE Advanced Energy Retrofit Guides

usageReduction.text: Retrofit remaining fluorescent or older LED fixtures to high-efficacy LEDs and add occupancy sensors in offices, conference rooms, restrooms, and support spaces, with daylight dimming on perimeter areas. Office lighting upgrades commonly reduce lighting energy 50-75% and also lower internal heat gains, reducing cooling load in Texas.
usageReduction.source: DOE Better Buildings: LED retrofit savings 60-75%; EIA CBECS 2018 office energy profiles

usageReduction.text: Use the utility rate structure to target peak demand reduction and procurement optimization: review interval data for coincident peak hours, shift noncritical loads outside late-afternoon summer peaks, and evaluate demand response or tariff alternatives under the LGS-2 class. With a blended rate of $0.1785/kWh and high monthly usage of 93,550 kWh, even modest demand reduction can materially reduce delivery and ERCOT volatility exposure.
usageReduction.source: Texas ERCOT demand-response guidance; Utility rate class LGS-2 tariff analysis; DOE Better Buildings peak demand management

procurement.text: In Texas/ERCOT, a fixed-price supply contract is usually the better base strategy for an office like this because it protects against summer volatility and budget risk; use a 12–24 month fixed term with layered renewal timing, and compare indexed only if the company can tolerate monthly swings. Given the current blended rate of $0.1785/kWh and 487 kW peak demand, the biggest opportunity is not chasing spot prices but locking competitive supply while actively reducing load before renewal.
procurement.source: ERCOT market data 2024; Texas commercial rate benchmarks; EIA Texas commercial electricity rates

procurement.text: Optimize supply cost by bidding the account to multiple Texas retail electric providers, requesting quotes on all-in fixed energy, indexed, and hybrid structures, and separating supply from TDU pass-throughs so you can compare apples-to-apples. For a large general service account, also evaluate block-and-index or partial-term staggering to avoid renewing all load at a single market high.
procurement.source: Texas REP pricing structures; ERCOT retail competition benchmarks; the team procurement best practices

procurement.text: Manage delivery cost by targeting peak-demand reduction, because in Texas the TDU portion and demand-related charges can materially affect the bill even when energy prices are low. Implement HVAC scheduling, optimum start/stop, unoccupied setbacks, and server room load management to trim summer peaks; even a modest reduction in peak kW can lower delivery-related charges and improve future quote pricing.
procurement.source: Texas TDU delivery charge structures; office building demand management benchmarks; commercial HVAC optimization studies

procurement.text: Enroll the site in ERCOT-compatible demand response or curtailable load programs through the REP/aggregator market, especially because the office operates mainly 8am–5pm weekdays and has flexible noncritical load during peak events. Demand response can create bill credits or event payments while also helping with ESG goals by reducing peak grid strain.
procurement.source: ERCOT demand response market participation data; Texas REP demand response program offerings

procurement.text: Time the next procurement 120–180 days before contract expiration and request quotes across multiple term lengths to capture seasonal ERCOT pricing, with summer start dates avoided when possible. For an office with a dedicated server room, pair a longer fixed term on base building load with operational controls for IT and HVAC, then revisit hedging or partial index exposure only if management wants upside participation.
procurement.source: ERCOT seasonal price volatility patterns; Texas commercial procurement timing benchmarks; the team contract strategy benchmarks

procurement.text: Prioritize operational efficiency measures alongside procurement: HVAC reset strategies, lighting controls, occupancy-based scheduling, and server room temperature setpoint optimization. In Texas office buildings, these measures commonly produce fast paybacks and can reduce the monthly spend base before the next supply bid, improving both cost and sustainability performance.
procurement.source: Texas office energy efficiency benchmarks; DOE commercial building optimization studies

alternativeGeneration.text: Rooftop solar appears financially viable for this 50,000 sq. ft. Texas office building: a roughly 85 kW system could produce about 142,800 kWh/year and save about $11,867/year, with an estimated simple payback of 8.6 years after the 30% ITC. Given the building’s 15 floors and likely limited roof area, confirm usable roof space and whether structural/mechanical obstructions reduce the installable capacity before moving forward.
alternativeGeneration.source: NREL PVWatts 2024 + LBNL Tracking the Sun 2024

alternativeGeneration.text: Because this is a daytime office with a dedicated server room and a high blended electric rate, pair solar with battery storage only if the utility tariff creates meaningful demand-charge reduction or if backup resilience is a priority; otherwise storage will usually lengthen payback in Texas. A targeted battery sized for peak shaving and server-room ride-through may make sense, but only after a load profile analysis confirms repeatable afternoon demand spikes.
alternativeGeneration.source: NREL PVWatts 2024 + Texas commercial tariff analysis

alternativeGeneration.text: This site is a stronger candidate for ownership than a PPA if the company can use the tax benefits or has access to a tax equity partner, because the estimated 8.6-year payback is solid for an office asset with ESG goals. If capital is constrained, a PPA can still work, but compare the PPA rate carefully against the current $0.1785/kWh blended rate and demand-charge exposure to ensure savings are real.

Community solar is likely a fallback option rather than the first choice here, since the building profile and Texas solar economics suggest rooftop solar should pencil out if roof conditions are adequate. Use community solar only if roof access, structural capacity, or lease constraints prevent installing the approximately 85 kW rooftop system.

email.subject: LoneStar Electric: 27% Estimated Energy Savings Opportunity
email.body:
Hi Ashwin,

Given LoneStar Electric’s role in the Texas market, your 50,000 sq. ft. office is a strong candidate for both operational energy savings and smarter procurement strategy. Based on the usage and spend profile shared, we estimate a potential 27% reduction in energy costs — approximately $60,624 in annual savings — with an expected payback period of about 6 months.

The most impactful opportunities appear to be:

1. Usage reduction measures: Targeted efficiency upgrades and controls optimization to reduce avoidable load during peak and occupied hours.
2. Procurement strategy: Reviewing REP contract structure, renewal timing, and ERCOT/TDU tariff exposure to reduce cost volatility and avoid unfavorable contract terms.
3. Alternative generation: Evaluating onsite or offsite generation options that may improve long-term cost certainty and resilience.

From a compliance standpoint, Texas does not currently have a statewide building performance standard comparable to NYC LL97/LL84/LL87, but local requirements in Austin, Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio should be monitored. ERCOT market exposure and utility/REP contract timing are the more immediate action items.

We recommend a detailed energy audit and procurement strategy session to validate the savings, prioritize measures, and map out a clear implementation path.

Would you be open to scheduling a 30-minute strategy call next week?

Best,
The our team Team

usageReduction.text: Audit the compressed air system for leaks, inappropriate pressure setpoints, and off-hours operation, then install automatic shutoff/controls so compressors only run when production needs them. In manufacturing facilities, compressed air is often one of the highest-cost utilities, and even modest reductions in pressure and runtime can cut electrical load quickly.
usageReduction.source: DOE Better Buildings Program: Compressed Air Best Practices; U.S. DOE Compressed Air System Assessment Tool

usageReduction.text: Optimize process heating and furnace operation by tightening temperature controls, repairing insulation/refractory, and adding schedule-based setbacks or shutdowns during non-production periods. Because this site runs two shifts, aligning furnace warm-up and cooldown to actual production windows can reduce gas use at the $1.12/therm New York commercial average and lower peak electric demand from auxiliary equipment.
usageReduction.source: DOE Better Buildings: Process Heating; DOE Industrial Assessment Centers (IAC)

usageReduction.text: Perform a New York tariff and interval-data review to separate energy, demand, delivery, and rider charges, then target the 500 kW peak with demand management controls. Shifting or staggering large motor starts, compressor cycling, and furnace auxiliary loads during the highest-demand intervals can reduce billed demand charges, which are often a major cost driver at this load profile.
usageReduction.source: NYSERDA FlexTech Program; Con Edison / NY utility interval-meter demand management guidance; EIA commercial and industrial rate benchmarks

usageReduction.text: Enroll in utility or NYSERDA demand response and peak-shaving programs and use the facility’s two-shift schedule to curtail noncritical loads during system peaks. A 50,000 sq. ft. industrial site with 500 kW peak demand is well suited for automated peak alerts, load shedding, and staged equipment shutdowns that lower both energy costs and sustainability footprint.
usageReduction.source: NYSERDA Demand Response Programs; DOE Better Buildings: Peak Demand Reduction

procurement.text: For this New York manufacturing site, prioritize a fixed-price electricity supply contract for 12-24 months while using interval data to verify whether the account is billed on a suitable commercial/industrial tariff. NY market volatility and the facility’s 500 kW peak load make fixed pricing the safer choice for budget certainty, with index pricing only considered for a smaller hedge portion if the company can actively manage usage.
procurement.source: EIA New York electricity rate data 2024; NYISO market conditions; the team procurement benchmarks

procurement.text: Review the utility tariff in detail to separate supply, delivery, demand, and rider charges, then target delivery-cost reductions through demand charge management, peak shaving, and power factor correction if applicable. At 500 kW peak demand, even modest reductions in peak coincident load can materially lower monthly delivery bills.
procurement.source: New York utility tariff structures; NY PSC rate design guidance; industrial demand charge benchmarks

procurement.text: Implement operational load shifting around compressed air and process heating/furnace cycles to reduce coincident peak demand and improve kW profile during the highest-cost intervals. Interval-data analytics and controls tuning are likely the fastest payback opportunities for a two-shift industrial facility with constant process loads.
procurement.source: Industrial demand management benchmarks; NYISO peak pricing patterns; compressed air efficiency best practices

procurement.text: Enroll in a demand response program through the utility or a NYISO/third-party curtailment provider if the facility can reliably shed 100-200 kW during called events. Manufacturing sites with flexible production schedules often earn meaningful incentive payments, and the participation can be aligned with ESG goals by demonstrating grid-supportive operations.
procurement.source: NYISO demand response programs; utility DR offerings in New York; CPower/Enel market participation benchmarks

procurement.text: For gas-fired process heating, bid natural gas supply competitively and consider a fixed gas term of 12 months if usage is stable; if loads vary materially, use a layered purchasing approach. New York gas prices are typically lower than electric volatility, but process heat savings often come from combustion tuning, insulation, and maintenance rather than commodity procurement alone.
procurement.source: EIA New York natural gas price data 2024; industrial gas procurement benchmarks

procurement.text: Coordinate contract timing to avoid peak summer and winter renewal windows when NY power prices can be less favorable; solicit quotes 60-120 days before expiration and compare fixed supply, indexed, and blended structures. For a single-site industrial account, a 24-month fixed deal with pricing triggers and re-openers is often the best balance of savings and risk control.
procurement.source: New York retail energy market benchmarks; NYISO seasonal pricing trends; the team contract timing best practices

alternativeGeneration.text: Rooftop solar is viable on this 50,000 sq. ft. New York manufacturing site, but the project is modest at roughly 85 kW due to roof area and would generate about 106,250 kWh/year. With an estimated post-ITC cost of $113,050 and a ~6-year simple payback, it can pencil out if the facility can use the output onsite and capture value through NY incentives/net metering or an attractive third-party PPA.
alternativeGeneration.source: NREL PVWatts 2024; LBNL Tracking the Sun 2024; DSIRE incentive database

alternativeGeneration.text: Because the site has a material 500 kW peak demand and two-shift operation, add battery storage only if interval data shows significant demand charges, peak shaving opportunity, or resilience value; storage is more likely to be justified as a demand-management tool paired with solar than as a standalone project. If demand charges are low, battery economics will likely be weak.
alternativeGeneration.source: NREL storage economics 2024; NYISO demand-response program information; utility tariff review

alternativeGeneration.text: A PPA is worth comparing against ownership here because the site has meaningful load but a relatively small rooftop PV system; a PPA can preserve capital and still deliver savings, but ownership likely offers better long-term economics if the company can use tax benefits or structure a direct purchase. Run both options against the actual NY tariff and incentive stack before deciding.
alternativeGeneration.source: DSIRE incentive database; NYSERDA solar program guidance; LBNL distributed solar market reports

alternativeGeneration.text: On-site CHP or fuel cells are not the first recommendation for this facility unless the process heating/furnace load is large, continuous, and well matched to thermal recovery needs. Given the information provided, prioritize energy efficiency, compressed-air optimization, and demand management first; then evaluate CHP only if a detailed heat-load analysis shows strong year-round thermal demand.
alternativeGeneration.source: DOE CHP Technical Assistance Partnerships; DOE Better Buildings

alternativeGeneration.text: If roof constraints, interconnection, or tariff economics reduce the project’s value, community solar is a solid fallback in New York and can still support ESG goals without on-site construction. It is especially useful if the facility cannot host the full 85 kW or if the corporate buyer wants simpler implementation.
alternativeGeneration.source: NYSERDA community solar guidance; DSIRE incentive database

complianceFlags.note: If this 50,000 sq. ft. facility is in New York City, annual energy and water benchmarking is required for buildings over 25,000 sq. ft., so the site should confirm filing responsibility and prepare yearly data collection.

If the facility is in NYC and qualifies as a covered building, buildings over 25,000 sq. ft. are subject to emissions limits and potential penalties for exceedances, so the site should assess current fuel/electricity emissions against applicable compliance periods.

complianceFlags.note: If this building is in NYC and exceeds 50,000 sq. ft., it is at the threshold for decennial energy audits and retro-commissioning, so the facility should confirm its audit year and compliance schedule.

complianceFlags.law: NYC Local Law 33 (Energy Efficiency Rating Label)
complianceFlags.note: If the site is in NYC and subject to benchmarking, it may also need to display a public energy efficiency grade label, which can affect ESG visibility and customer perception.

complianceFlags.law: New York State Energy Conservation Construction Code
complianceFlags.note: Any future equipment, envelope, lighting, or process-related project should be checked against state energy code requirements, especially for retrofits at an industrial facility with significant process loads.
complianceFlags.source: New York State Energy Conservation Construction Code (current adopted code)

savingsBreakdown.methodology: Compressed-air leak repair and controls, process heating/furnace insulation and scheduling, and demand-management tuning reduce electric, gas, and billed peak-demand usage for the two-shift operation.

Fixed-price electricity and gas procurement, tariff validation, interval-data review, and demand-response enrollment capture the specialist-estimated procurement savings while improving budget certainty in New York.
An approximately 85 kW rooftop solar system producing about 106,250 kWh per year offsets onsite purchases and supports ESG goals using New York solar economics and incentives.

email.subject: Energy savings opportunity for test’s NY manufacturing facility
email.body:
Hi abc2,

Given test’s 50,000 sq. ft. manufacturing/industrial facility in New York and current energy spend of approximately $20,000 per month, our team reviewed the opportunity to reduce operating costs while strengthening compliance readiness.

Based on the initial findings, we estimate potential energy savings of about 14%, or roughly $33,600 per year, with an expected payback period of just 8 months.

The most impactful next opportunities appear to be:

1. Usage reduction measures to lower demand and improve efficiency across core facility operations.
2. Procurement strategy optimization to ensure test is buying energy under the most favorable available terms.
3. Alternative generation evaluation, including options that may reduce grid dependence and improve long-term cost stability.

There are also several compliance items that require attention, including NYC Local Law 84 benchmarking, Local Law 97 building emissions limits, and Local Law 87 energy audit/retro-commissioning requirements. Local Law 33 and NY State Energy Conservation Construction Code items should continue to be monitored.

We recommend a detailed energy audit and strategy session to validate savings, prioritize measures, and map out a compliance and implementation plan.

Would you be open to scheduling a 30-minute discussion next week?

Best,
The our team Team
